title: Exercising early on a tree
objectives: Price an American put by checking early exercise at every node.
Explain why an American call on a share without dividends is never exercised early.

screens.title: Hold or exercise?
screens.prose: An **American** put may be exercised at any node, not only at expiry. This one is struck at £100, on the two-step tree with $q = 0.625$ and $r = 5\%$. You hold it at the £80 node.

state.caption: Put payoffs at year 2; holding at £80 is worth £15.24

screens.question: Holding on is worth £15.24, by backward induction. What should you do?

options.text: Exercise: sell at £100 a share worth £80, and take £20
Hold: £15.24 is the fair value of the put
options.why: £15.24 is the value if you must wait. Exercising pays £20 now, more than waiting is worth.

options.text: Hold: the put could pay £36 next year
options.why: £36 comes only after another fall, and a year later. Weighted and discounted, waiting is worth only £15.24.

options.text: It makes no difference
options.why: Exercising pays £20 and holding is worth £15.24: a gap of £4.76.

hints.text: What does exercising pay at the £80 node?
Exercising sells for £100 a share worth £80.
Exercise pays $100 - 80 = 20$. Compare that with the £15.24 of holding.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what exercising pays now with what holding is worth.

byKey.fair: £15.24 is the value if you must wait. Exercising pays £20 now, more than waiting is worth.
byKey.36: £36 comes only after another fall, and a year later. Weighted and discounted, waiting is worth only £15.24.

explain.text: Exercising gives £20 now; holding is worth £15.24. The holder takes the larger, so the American put is worth £20 at the £80 node. Deep in the money, receiving £100 a year early beats the chance of more.

screens.title: Hold against exercise
screens.prose: You just compared two numbers. The value of holding is the **continuation value**: the $q$-weighted, discounted value of the next two nodes. The **exercise value** is $\max(100 - S, 0)$ now.
screens.question: Fill in the table for the two year-1 nodes.

hints.text: From £120 the put goes to £0 or £4 a year later.
At £120 the put is out of the money, so exercising pays nothing.
Hold at £120: $(0.625 \times 0 + 0.375 \times 4)/1.05 = 1.43$. Each node keeps the larger value.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute hold and exercise at each node, then keep the larger.

byKey.r0c1: From £120 the put goes to £0 or £4: $0.375 \times 4 / 1.05 = 1.43$.
byKey.r0c2: At £120 the put is out of the money: $100 - 120 < 0$, so exercising pays nothing.
byKey.r0c3: Take the larger of hold, £1.43, and exercise, £0.
byKey.r1c3: Take the larger of hold, £15.24, and exercise, £20.

explain.text: At £120 you hold: £1.43 beats £0. At £80 you exercise: £20 beats £15.24. Each node keeps the larger of its continuation and exercise values.

screens.title: Back to today
screens.prose: Step back to today with the American values: £1.43 at £120 and £20 at £80. Exercising today would pay $\max(100 - 100, 0) = 0$.
screens.question: What is the American put worth today?

hints.text: Use the same rule as at year 1: continuation against exercise.
The next nodes are worth £1.43 and £20.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight £1.43 and £20 by 0.625 and 0.375, then discount.

byKey.european: You used £15.24 at the £80 node, the value if you must wait. The American holder exercises there for £20.
byKey.one-step: You left out the £120 node’s £1.43. Both next nodes count.
byKey.no-disc: You weighted correctly but did not discount by 1.05.

explain.text: $(0.625 \times 1.43 + 0.375 \times 20)/1.05 = 7.99$, against £6.29 for the European put. The right to exercise early is worth £1.70 here. Today’s exercise value is £0, so today you hold.

screens.title: The maximum only at the end
screens.prose: A colleague’s code takes $\max(100 - S, 0)$ at year 2, then discounts back with $q$. It returns £6.29, and she labels it “American put”.
screens.question: What has her code priced?

options.text: The European put: it never compares holding with exercising at year 1
The American put: the max at expiry covers early exercise
options.why: You took the maximum only at the leaves. At £80 holding is worth £15.24 but exercising pays £20, and the code never asks.

options.text: The American put, less a year of interest
options.why: The gap is not interest. $7.99 - 6.29 = 1.70$ comes from exercising at £80.

options.text: An American call
options.why: The payoff is $\max(100 - S, 0)$, a put’s. Only the early-exercise check is missing.

hints.text: Where in her code could early exercise happen?
Look at the £80 node: £15.24 against £20.
Her code takes a max only at expiry. That is the European rule.

feedback.correct: A max at expiry alone is the European rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether her code ever compares with exercising before expiry.

byKey.american: You took the maximum only at the leaves. At £80 holding is worth £15.24 but exercising pays £20, and the code never asks.

explain.text: Taking the max only at expiry is the European rule. The American check sits at every node: $V = \max(\text{hold}, \text{exercise})$. Here it lifts the £80 node from £15.24 to £20, and today from £6.29 to £7.99.

screens.title: A call never goes early
screens.prose: Now an American call struck at £100 on the same tree. The share pays no dividends. Holding the call is worth £26.19 at £120 and £15.59 today, from the last lesson.

state.caption: Call: payoffs at year 2, hold values before

screens.question: Where, if anywhere, should you exercise the call before year 2?

options.text: Nowhere: holding beats exercising at every node
At £120: it is £20 in the money
options.why: Exercising pays £20, but holding is worth £26.19. You would give up £6.19.

options.text: Today, to lock in the price
options.why: Exercising today pays $\max(100 - 100, 0) = 0$, against £15.59 for holding.

options.text: At £80, to stop further losses
options.why: At £80 the call is out of the money: exercising pays nothing.

hints.text: At each node, compare $S - 100$ with the hold value.
At £120, exercise pays £20 and holding is worth £26.19.
Holding wins at £120, today and at £80, so you never exercise early.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare exercise, $S - 100$, with the hold value at each node.

byKey.u: Exercising pays £20, but holding is worth £26.19. You would give up £6.19.

explain.text: Holding is worth at least $S - K/(1 + r)$, which beats $S - K$ whenever $r > 0$. So exercising early gives away the interest on the strike. On a share without dividends the American call equals the European, as the options course found.

screens.title: The American rule
screens.prose: At every node you compared two values and kept the larger. For a put struck at $K$: $$V = \max\left(\dfrac{qV_{\text{up}} + (1-q)V_{\text{down}}}{1 + r},\ K - S\right).$$ The nodes where exercise wins form the **early exercise region**.
screens.question: Why is an American option always worth at least its European twin?

options.text: Its holder can always choose never to exercise early
Its tree has more nodes
options.why: Both use the same tree. The difference is the choice at each node.

options.text: It pays more at expiry
options.why: At expiry both pay $\max(K - S, 0)$. Only the earlier choice differs.

options.text: Early exercise always pays more
options.why: At £120 exercising the put pays £0 against £1.43 for holding. Exercise is used only when it wins.

feedback.correct: Never exercising early copies the European option.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what the American holder can do that the European holder cannot.

explain.text: Never exercising early copies the European option, so the American is worth at least as much. The max can only raise a node’s value. On our tree: £7.99 against £6.29.

screens.title: No interest
screens.prose: Now set $r = 0$ on the same tree. Then $q = \dfrac{1 - 0.8}{1.2 - 0.8} = 0.5$, and nothing is discounted.
screens.question: What is the American put worth today?

widget.label: American put today, in £
widget.accept: £11.00: at £80 hold and exercise are both £20, so $0.5 \times 2 + 0.5 \times 20 = 11$.

hints.text: Compare hold and exercise at £80 first.
At £80, holding gives $0.5 \times 4 + 0.5 \times 36 = 20$, and exercising gives £20.
Today: $0.5 \times 2 + 0.5 \times 20 = 11$, against £0 for exercising.

feedback.correct: £11.00, the same as the European put.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $r = 0$, use $q = 0.5$ and no discounting.

byKey.exercise-only: £10 would need the £120 node to be worth nothing. Holding there is worth £2.
byKey.discounted: You divided by 1.05. With $r = 0$ nothing is discounted.

explain.text: At £80 holding gives exactly the exercise value, £20. With no interest, waiting costs nothing, so exercising early never strictly gains. The American put equals the European: £11.00.

screens.title: Where to exercise
screens.prose: This is the four-step tree from the last lesson: £100, $\sigma = 20\%$, quarterly steps, $r = 5\%$. An American put is struck at £100. Each node shows its price and its hold value.

state.caption: Exercise pays $100 - S$ at each node

screens.question: Tap every node before expiry where you should exercise.

hints.text: At each node, compare $100 - S$ with the hold value.
Only nodes below £100 can be worth exercising.
£74.08: 25.92 against 24.68. £90.48 after three quarters: 9.52 against 8.27. £81.87: 18.13 against 16.88.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At each node below £100, compare $100 - S$ with the hold value.

byKey.same-price: You exercised at £90.48 after one quarter. There holding is worth £10.58, more than the £9.52 exercise pays.
byKey.n10: At £90.48 after one quarter, holding is worth £10.58, more than the £9.52 exercise pays.
byKey.n21: At £100 exercising pays nothing, and holding is worth £4.34.

explain.text: Exercise wins at £74.08 and £90.48 after three quarters, and at £81.87 after two. At £90.48 after one quarter you hold: more time left makes waiting worth more. The region is low prices late in the option’s life; the put is worth £5.88, against £5.09 European.

screens.title: Callable bonds and mortgages
screens.prose: A firm’s bond lets the firm buy it back at £100 on any coupon date: a **callable bond**. Rates have fallen, so the bond’s payments are now worth £104. A homeowner who may repay a mortgage early holds the same kind of right.

rows: Call now: buy back for £100 debt worth £104
Wait: keep the right to call later

state.caption: A callable bond, after rates have fallen

screens.question: What should the firm do on this date?

options.text: Call the bond: saving £4 now beats the £2.50 that waiting is worth
Wait: rates may fall further
options.why: Waiting is worth £2.50 to the firm; calling saves £4 now. As at the £80 node, take the larger.

options.text: Call only at maturity
options.why: That would make the call European. The firm may call on any coupon date, so it checks each one.

options.text: Never call: the firm should keep paying its coupons
options.why: Calling replaces debt worth £104 with £100 of cash. Keeping it costs the firm £4.

hints.text: This is the same comparison as at each node of the put’s tree.
Exercise is worth £4 to the firm; waiting is worth £2.50.
Take the larger: call the bond.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what calling saves now with what waiting is worth.

byKey.wait: Waiting is worth £2.50 to the firm; calling saves £4 now. As at the £80 node, take the larger.
byKey.maturity: That would make the call European. The firm may call on any coupon date, so it checks each one.

explain.text: The firm holds an American call on its own debt, and here exercise wins: £4 against £2.50. A mortgage borrower repays early for the same reason when rates fall. Pricing either needs a tree of interest rates, with this check at every node.

ideas: At every node an American holder compares the continuation value with the exercise value and keeps the larger.
An American option is worth at least its European twin. With zero interest, the American put equals the European.
An American call on a share without dividends is never exercised early; an American put deep in the money is.

formula.name: American put on a tree
formula.note: The max goes at every node, not only at expiry.

summary.trap: A max taken only at expiry prices the European put: £6.29, not £7.99.

quiz.question: What is the American put worth today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare hold and exercise at each year-1 node, then step back.

byKey.european: You kept £24.76 at £80. Exercising there pays $110 - 80 = 30$, which is more.

quiz.prose: A trader holds an American call on a share that pays no dividends. The share has risen far above the strike.
quiz.question: What should the trader do to cash in?

options.text: Sell the call rather than exercise it
Exercise it now, before the share falls
options.why: Exercising gets $S - K$. The call is worth at least $S - K/(1 + r)$, so selling it gets more.

options.text: Hold until expiry, whatever happens
options.why: Holding is fine, but the trader wanted to cash in. Selling captures the full value now.

options.text: Exercise or sell: they are worth the same
options.why: They differ by the interest on the strike. Exercising pays the strike early.

feedback.correct: The call sells for more than it pays on exercise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $S - K$ with the call’s value, at least $S - K/(1 + r)$.

explain.text: An American call on a non-dividend share is worth at least $S - K/(1 + r)$, more than the $S - K$ exercise pays. So exercising early throws away value. Selling the call keeps it.

quiz.prose: At one node of a tree the share is £70. An American put struck at £100 has a hold value of £27.50 there.
quiz.question: What is the American put worth at that node?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the larger of hold and exercise.

byKey.hold: £27.50 is the hold value. Exercising pays £30, so the holder exercises.
byKey.sum: You added the two. The holder gets one or the other, so take the larger.

explain.text: Exercise pays $100 - 70 = 30$, which beats holding at £27.50. So the node is in the early exercise region and is worth £30.

quiz.prose: Interest rates are zero. A European put on a share is worth £6.40.
quiz.question: What is the American put with the same strike and expiry worth?

options.text: More than £6.40, because early exercise is a right
options.why: With no interest, getting the strike early earns nothing, so the right is worth nothing extra.

options.text: Less than £6.40
options.why: An American option is never worth less than its European twin: just never exercise early.

options.text: It cannot be known without the tree
options.why: At zero rates holding is always worth at least exercising, so the two values agree on any tree.

feedback.correct: At zero rates the American put equals the European.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what early exercise gains when money earns no interest.

explain.text: With $r = 0$ the hold value is an average of future values, never less than $K - S$ today. So early exercise never strictly gains. The American put is worth the same £6.40.
